A.best_element: Calendar correctness details: base32hex event-id rule (^[a-v0-9]{5,1024}$, so an 'sgw' prefix is invalid), reminders count back from event start, and a personal-use setup guide (publish to 'In production' without verification, then re-authorize) to escape the 7-day Testing refresh-token expiry.
A.biggest_weakness: Lopsided toward Google auth/calendar: highlight/hide, scheduling and sniping get one line each, with no prior art, no framework guidance, thin bid safety, and no mention of SGW's Terms of Use prohibition.

C.best_element: Non-negotiable engineering rules: ports-and-adapters with injected Clock/Http/Storage/Alarms, tests-first plus a gate command per task, test-only hooks compiled out with CI proof, a manifest-permission snapshot, and a threat-model table where every control has a proving test.
C.biggest_weakness: Treats SGW's ToS stance as unknown when the Terms of Use explicitly ban scripts and extensions; omits the naive Pacific-time endTime and the server-clock endpoint; its Firefox host-permission note predates Firefox 127; thin prior art.

D.best_element: A Site Adapter layer (DOM/API/Session/Clock) with versioned selector and endpoint config and a healthCheck() that disables all write automation on drift, fed by a Task-0 read-only recon spike whose fixtures every downstream task consumes instead of the live site.
D.biggest_weakness: Mandates Playwright e2e on Firefox (Playwright cannot load Firefox extensions) and suggests the archived webextension-polyfill; says little about closed-browser reliability, companion options or Calendar OAuth token expiry.

E.best_element: 'Hiding is never silent' UX (collapsed stubs, an 'N hidden · show' bar, a per-card Why?, one-click undo), plus the anecdote that favoriting no-bid items attracts bidders, which leads to a per-watch local-only option. Also the richest prior-art list.
E.biggest_weakness: Treating 'UX direction as requirements' (side panel, onboarding, WCAG, dark mode, wireframes, microcopy) bloats scope; platform and OAuth facts are thin, and some claims are stated without flags (no clock extension, 15-auction cap, notes up to 500 chars vs 256 elsewhere).

F.best_element: Snipe-engine depth: lowest-RTT clock-offset sampling, a T-60s re-check, retrying only when the bid provably never arrived, an outcome taxonomy, a total-open-exposure cap, and a mock buyerapi with injectable latency, skew, token expiry and soft-close.
F.biggest_weakness: Lopsided toward the nice-to-have sniping: SPA injection, the rules engine and Calendar OAuth are barely covered; it also asks for Playwright E2E on Firefox and flags Dashboard/GetCurrentTime as unverified although it is in the live site bundle.

rationale: C edges D because its non-negotiable engineering rules (ports-and-adapters, tests-first tasks with gate commands, CI lanes, compiled-out test hooks, a threat model with proving tests) map most directly onto isolated parallel workers plus extensive testing, and its tooling facts are correct (Playwright extension E2E is Chromium-only; Firefox goes through BiDi, Selenium or web-ext). D has the best site recon and the Terms of Use finding, but it mandates an impossible Firefox Playwright lane and is thinner on OAuth and closed-browser reliability. C's main gap, listing the ToS as unknown, is offset by its strict bidding gates and its open question on ToS comfort.
